analysis.one_liner: Raises taxes on corporations that move their headquarters offshore on paper while keeping their business in the US.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no further action before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Some US companies move their legal headquarters to a low-tax country while keeping their executives, employees, and operations in the United States — a practice called corporate inversion. This bill would change the tax code so those companies are still treated as American for tax purposes: if more than half the company's stock ends up with its former US shareholders, or if its management stays primarily in the US with significant American business activity, it pays US taxes like any domestic company. The change would apply to tax years ending after May 8, 2014.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and US-based companies that pay their full tax bills, since companies that only pretend to move offshore would keep paying US taxes on their American business. That revenue could otherwise fund public services or reduce deficits borne by everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: It treats a foreign company as American for tax purposes when former shareholders of the US company own more than 50% of it after the deal, or when its management and control stay primarily in the United States with significant US business activity.
It applies the rules retroactively to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, and closes a current-law loophole that only counts deals where 60% or more of shares are held by former US shareholders.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that would otherwise save taxes by redomiciling abroad while keeping most operations and management in the US; they would owe US corporate tax on their income again.

drawbacks.text: Companies with substantial business activity in their foreign country of organization are exempted, so multinationals with real overseas operations could still relocate and qualify for the exception.
Raising taxes on US-headquartered multinationals could, in the view of critics, push investment, headquarters, or jobs abroad rather than raise revenue — a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific tax-avoidance strategy that shifts costs onto other taxpayers, and its 50% ownership plus management-and-control tests are written to catch inversion deals while exempting companies with genuinely substantial foreign operations. The main trade-off is economic: higher US tax bills for multinationals could reduce investment or jobs in the US, and some economists argue corporate rates are best lowered rather than enforced more aggressively. On balance the bill is a straightforward closing of a loophole, but it received no committee consideration, so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 7, 2024, and read twice on the Senate floor.
Referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation.
The committee took no further action; no hearings, markups, or votes are recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that have inverted or plan to, which keep the current tax rules that let them reincorporate abroad while staying US-based in practice.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 10 senators (9 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Reed, Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Sanders, Hirono, Duckworth, Van Hollen, and Baldwin.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor agenda and did not bring the bill up; no action was taken beyond committee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced in the Senate.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations seeking to redomicile abroad
industries.note: The bill would strip the tax benefit of inversion deals and treat inverted companies as fully domestic for US tax purposes, raising their US tax bills. It died in committee, so no effect was ever realized.

Companies that remain US-headquartered face no new rules and avoid competing against inverted rivals' lower tax bills, but they would face higher US taxes on foreign income under the stricter inverted-corporation tests.
